chunks.title: knowledge_assistant
chunks.text: A local-first RAG system for querying your own documents — FastAPI and LangChain over Ollama (Llama 3), with pgvector for retrieval. The problem Most RAG demos assume you're fine sending your documents to someone else's API. knowledge assistant doesn't: it's a local-first system for querying your own PDFs, running entirely on your own machine — no document leaves it, and there's no per-query API bill. Architecture Two separate pipelines share one vector store. Ingestion loads PDFs from a local directory, splits them into chunks with a recursive text splitter, embeds each chunk with an Ollama embedding model, and stores the vectors in Postgres via the pgvector extension.

chunks.title: knowledge_assistant
chunks.text: The query side is a FastAPI endpoint: it embeds the incoming question, retrieves the nearest chunks from pgvector , and runs the result through a LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) chain that augments the prompt with the retrieved context before calling Llama 3 through Ollama. Decisions Ollama over a hosted LLM API. Everything runs locally — no OpenAI or Anthropic key, no cost per query, no document ever leaving the machine it's running on. The tradeoff is throughput: a local model on consumer hardware won't serve concurrent users the way a hosted API scales, which is fine for a personal document assistant and would be the wrong call for something meant to serve traffic.

chunks.title: knowledge_assistant
chunks.text: Postgres + pgvector over a dedicated vector database. One database to run and back up instead of two separate systems (a relational store for metadata and a standalone vector DB). For a corpus that fits comfortably in Postgres, that's less operational surface for no real capability loss. LCEL over hand-rolled prompt strings. LangChain's expression language composes the retrieval step and the generation step into one declarative chain rather than manually string-formatting a prompt with retrieved context spliced in. What I'd change TODO(lasal): this is the part only you can fill in honestly — what broke during ingestion or retrieval, any latency or scale numbers you've actually observed, and what you'd do differently with what you know now.

chunks.title: knowledge_assistant
chunks.text: Real specifics here, whenever you have them, are worth more than anything written from just reading the code.

chunks.title: NatCon Website
chunks.text: Official website for AIESEC in Sri Lanka's National Conference 2026 — homepage, countdown, registration, and a merch store. The problem AIESEC in Sri Lanka's National Conference 2026 needed a live site — registration, delegate room lookup, a merch store with checkout, and sponsor/partner pages — on a fixed date that doesn't move. Starting from a blank Next.js app on a conference timeline means building routing, a cart context, and a checkout flow from zero before writing a single line of NatCon-specific content.

chunks.title: NatCon Website
chunks.text: Starting point: a fork, not a rewrite This is a fork of [yashbim/nlds-website](https://github.com/yashbim/nlds-website), the previous year's conference site — same underlying stack (Next.js, Supabase, a cart context, a merch store), reused deliberately instead of rebuilt, because the previous year's team had already solved the boring, load-bearing parts: routing, a working checkout flow, a partner-logo grid. Forking meant NatCon 2026 could spend its build time on what was actually new, not on re-deriving a shopping cart. What "new" turned out to mean, comparing against the upstream repo directly: 75 commits, 146 files touched, +3,679/−1,787 lines.

chunks.title: NatCon Website
chunks.text: What actually changed A delegate room-lookup page ( /rooms ) that didn't exist upstream — a 767-line rewrite of the rooms component alone, for finding which room a delegate is assigned to. A title-partner page and component ( TitlePartner.tsx , 229 new lines) for NatCon's top-tier sponsor, absent from the base site. Registration handled as three real states instead of one: open, closed, and "opening soon" (a new RegistrationsOpeningSoon component) — because a conference registration page has a real lifecycle before and after the window is live, not just a single static form.

chunks.title: NatCon Website
chunks.text: The store, checkout, and order-confirmation flow rewritten , wired to Resend for the confirmation email rather than the upstream implementation, alongside a full replacement of merch product photography and partner logos for NatCon's own sponsors — the previous year's assets don't carry over to a different event. Kept current on the stack : Next.js was upgraded from 15.4.6 to 16.1.3 partway through, not left on whatever version the fork started on. Decisions Fork over rewrite. The honest tradeoff: inheriting an existing codebase's structure (and its rough edges) in exchange for a working checkout flow and routing on day one, instead of a cleaner from-scratch architecture that would have cost real time a fixed-date conference site doesn't have.

chunks.title: Breast Cancer Detection Model
chunks.text: Coursework project predicting mortality outcome and survival months for breast cancer patients from a ~4,000-patient clinical dataset — classification and regression models compared head to head. Classification accuracy: 85.0%. Classification AUC: 0.68. Survival regression RMSE: 22.9 months What this actually predicts The repo is named "detection," but it's worth being precise: this isn't detecting whether a tumor is malignant from imaging. It's predicting outcomes for patients already diagnosed — whether a patient survives ( Mortality Status ) and how many months they survive ( Survival Months ) — from a clinical dataset of 4,024 breast cancer patients: tumor stage, grade, hormone-receptor status, age, and node counts.

chunks.title: Breast Cancer Detection Model
chunks.text: Architecture Two tasks share the same cleaned dataset: a classification pass predicting mortality outcome (Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, and KNN, each grid-searched, combined into a voting ensemble), and a regression pass predicting survival months (a fully-grown decision tree compared against a pruned one). The result — and a data leak worth naming An earlier pass of the notebook trains the classifier on Survival Months as an input feature and reports 88.9% accuracy. That number doesn't hold up: Survival Months is a near-direct proxy for the mortality label itself — a patient with very few survival months is, almost by definition, one who died.

chunks.title: Breast Cancer Detection Model
chunks.text: Training on it isn't predicting mortality from clinical features, it's mostly reading the answer off an adjacent column. A later pass drops Survival Months from the classifier's inputs. That's the honest number: - Classification accuracy: 85.0% (voting ensemble of Logistic Regression + KNN), AUC 0.68 - Survival regression: RMSE 22.9 months (pruned decision tree — the fully-grown tree overfit badly enough to score a negative R², meaning it did worse than just predicting the average) An AUC of 0.68 is real but modest — noticeably short of the leaked run's apparent performance, which is exactly the point: the gap between 88.9% and 85.0% is the size of the leak, not a modeling improvement lost.

chunks.title: Breast Cancer Detection Model
chunks.text: What I'd change Pruning mattered more than model choice here — the fully-grown decision tree overfitting to a negative R² while the pruned version reached 0.019 is a bigger swing than the difference between any two classifiers tried. Worth trying next: a regularized model (Ridge/Lasso) for the regression side instead of a single tree, and checking whether other columns carry similar leakage before trusting any accuracy number that looks unusually good.
